profileSections.heading: Teaching, trust, and watching a family grow
profileSections.text: Ronald Shiell's West Dermatology biography puts teaching and family life alongside his surgical work. It recalls his time leading the dermatology division at Upstate Medical University in Syracuse, where he taught students pursuing medicine and directed the university's Mohs surgery center. Away from those responsibilities, he describes the pleasure of watching his two sons have fun, change, and grow. His own account of practice starts with imagining himself in the patient's position: he wants people to feel comfortable with him and his staff. That is his stated approach, not a promise about anyone's experience or outcome.

profileSections.text: For Carla Nip-Sakamoto, returning to Hawaii was also a family decision. Burns School of Medicine, and other nonprofit organizations. Away from the office, it names travel, time with family, and walks with her Papillon, Kona. profileSections.heading: Asking where he might belong
profileSections.text: Glenn Zellman tells his own story on Arizona Dermatology's website. He left Oceanside, New York, at 17, studied in North Carolina, and later trained in Houston. He remembers clinics where specialists worked together and patients arrived with conditions he had previously known from textbooks. When he began considering Arizona, he asked colleagues and friends in the pharmaceutical industry where he might practice. Several pointed him toward Arizona Dermatology. His account describes finding a team whose intellectual interests and approach to patient care felt compatible with his own. Those are his reflections on choosing a workplace, not independent evidence of better care.

profileSections.heading: Returning to the people who first taught him
profileSections.text: Peter Sigal's Arizona Dermatology biography describes a deliberate return to Arizona, rather than simply the next stop after training. Raised in Marietta, Georgia, he studied American history before medical school in Arizona and later worked and trained in New Jersey and Michigan. He chose to come back to practice with his original mentors, Dr. Ko and Dr. Ebner. His account also recalls learning Spanish while caring for predominantly Hispanic patients during his internship.
